ameliorate

uh-MEEL-yuh-rayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To ameliorate is to make a bad or unsatisfactory situation better.

International aid shipments helped ameliorate the food shortage in the weeks after the earthquake.

Example

New labor laws were passed to ameliorate the dangerous working conditions that factory inspectors had documented for years.

Ameliorate describes a gradual, often deliberate improvement to a bad situation -- it rarely means a problem is fixed completely.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

improve: To improve is the everyday, all-purpose word for making anything better -- a recipe, a grade, an already strong team -- whether or not it was ever bad. To ameliorate is narrower: it means partly easing a situation that is genuinely bad, and it never promises a complete fix.

better: To better something is simply to raise it above where it stood -- runners better their times; schools work to better test scores. To ameliorate applies only when something is bad or unsatisfactory: you can ameliorate a housing crisis, but not a personal record.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

worsen: to make or become worse

aggravate: to make a problem or situation worse

Where it sits · how big the improvement is

tweak → ameliorate → revolutionize

tweak vs. ameliorate: Tweak means to make a small adjustment or minor improvement, less significant than ameliorate.

revolutionize vs. ameliorate: Revolutionize means to completely transform something for the better, a far more dramatic change than simply ameliorating it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — a-: to, toward (Latin ad-)

root — melior-: better (Latin melior, comparative of bonus, 'good')

suffix — -ate: to make (Latin -atus)

Put it together: Ameliorate comes from a- ('to') + melior ('better') + -ate ('to make') -- literally 'to make better.' Latin melior doesn't survive as its own common English word, so there's no everyday root_mcq word to quiz here.

Use the root in a new word: meliorism: His editorials were famous for their stubborn meliorism.
